scenes.heading: Why atoms share electrons
scenes.narration: Atoms rarely sit alone. When two of them meet, they can lock together by sharing electrons, and understanding why that sharing happens explains almost every molecule around you right now.

scenes.heading: Sharing fills the shell
scenes.narration: In a covalent bond neither atom gives an electron away. Both contribute, and the shared pair counts for each of them, letting both reach a filled outer shell or octet.

scenes.heading: Lower energy means stability
scenes.narration: Here is the real reason. Two separate hydrogen atoms hold more energy than one bonded pair, so the bonded state is lower energy, and lower energy simply means more stable.

scenes.heading: Balancing pull and push
scenes.narration: Two forces settle the distance. Each nucleus pulls on the shared electron pair, while the two nuclei push each other apart, and the bond length is where that balance rests.

scenes.heading: Sharing for stability
scenes.narration: So atoms form covalent bonds by sharing electrons to complete an outer shell, reaching a lower energy and more stable arrangement, as seen in hydrogen gas, water and methane.

points: Shared pairs fill the outer shell
